title: Chapter 121 — Leading the Trade Desk & The Multi-Engine Floor
intro: The trade desk as a business unit and managing the specialist.

sections.title: Trade as a Business Unit
sections.content:
The trade desk is not a side project. It is a business unit with its own pipeline, its own revenue targets, its own account relationships, and its own operational requirements.

As a leader, you manage the trade desk the same way you manage the retail floor — with metrics, coaching, and accountability. Track trade revenue, account growth, quote-to-close ratio, and delivery satisfaction separately from retail.

sections.title: Managing the Trade Specialist
sections.content:
The trade specialist needs different management than the floor rep. They need autonomy to manage account relationships on their own schedule. They need pricing authority within defined boundaries. They need priority access to delivery scheduling.

But they also need accountability. Are they growing their accounts? Are they prospecting new ones? Is their share of wallet increasing? The quarterly account review is as important for the trade specialist as the weekly one-on-one is for the floor rep.

sections.title: The Multi-Engine Floor
sections.content:
A healthy store has two revenue engines — retail and trade. When retail is slow, trade keeps the revenue flowing. When trade has a quiet quarter, retail fills the gap.

The leader's job is to keep both engines running. Do not let trade cannibalize retail attention. Do not let retail emergencies pull the trade specialist off their accounts. Set boundaries, allocate resources, and measure both engines independently.

The store that masters both engines is resilient. The one that relies on only one is vulnerable.
